How to use Cosmos to Core

  • Journey through time: the Journey button at the top walks through 49 stops in order, from the Big Bang to today, with pictures, 3D stories and a check question at each. Use Next and Back (or the ← → keys).
  • Scroll, pinch, or drag the ruler on the left to zoom from Earth’s surface out to the edge of the observable universe.
  • Drag the scene to rotate. Tap labels and placemarks to learn more and open activities.
  • The Here tab lists the standards that fit the scale you’re looking at. The Standards tab holds all 19, each with an activity, the full standard, and its core ideas.
  • Choose Regents or Honors at the top. Content marked Honors goes beyond what the Regents exam assesses. In Regents mode it is tucked away behind a dashed “Honors extension” button you can still open.
  • The Practice tab has Regents-style clusters for every standard and every cluster from the released Earth and Space Sciences Regents exams. Tap a placemark and choose “Practice questions” to practice that place’s topics.
  • Labs: cut Earth or the Sun open and tap a layer, or open the full-screen labs (Inside Earth lab button, or the buttons in the panel) to explore layers, convection, earthquake waves, ridges and subduction, energy flow and fusion.
  • Reference Tables: look for the yellow RT boxes. They link to the matching pages of the 2026 Earth and Space Sciences Reference Tables.
  • Run a simulation: green ▶ buttons start a process (accretion, flux melting, earthquake waves and more). The Labs tab lists them all.
  • Where I live: the Labs tab (or the “Where I live (NY)” button under the globe) finds your New York town and explains its landscape, bedrock, glacial history, environment and nearby case studies.
  • Latitude & longitude: turn on the grid under the globe, point at Earth to read coordinates, or type coordinates to fly there.
  • New labs: Sun, Earth and Moon (phases, eclipses, tides), Atmosphere and ocean (global winds, El Niño and La Niña), and Milankovitch cycles in Climate futures. Turn on “Wind belts” under the globe to see the planetary winds.
  • Up close: keep zooming in on Earth (or tap a placemark) to see a 3D block of what is there: ridges, trenches, volcanoes, glaciated New York landscapes, ice sheets and more. Zoom further to tilt toward the ground; drag to look around.
  • Simulations on the globe: the Labs tab lists simulations that play out on the 3D Earth (the Ice Age, winds, El Niño, warming, earthquake waves, drifting continents).
  • Keyboard: + and − zoom, arrow keys rotate, Home returns to Earth.
